title: Healing hymns of the Atharvaveda

confidence.note: No Vedic text can be dated absolutely; the Atharvaveda is placed after c. 1100 BCE mainly because it is the first text to mention iron. The hymns themselves are well preserved, but identifying takman with malaria is an interpretation, and so is any link to later Ayurveda.

summary: India's oldest medical words are spells: hymns that flatter, bribe and banish takman, a fever-demon that strikes cold, then burning hot, on a regular cycle.
body: Some of the oldest medical words in India are spells. The Atharvaveda, a hymn collection compiled early in India's Iron Age, holds charms against takman, a fever-demon that comes cold, then deliriously hot, returns on the morrow or on the third day, and turns bodies yellow. Its 1897 translator thought this suggested malaria. Healers paid the demon homage, begged it to go to foreign peoples, and invoked plants such as kushtha, 'born upon the mountains'. Whether classical Ayurveda grew from this lore is doubtful: Dominik Wujastyk argues that the supposed parallels break down.

links.note: Ayurveda's link to Vedic healing is contested.

title: The Charaka Samhita

confidence.note: Meulenbeld's window of about 100 BCE to 150–200 CE for Caraka is widely accepted, but it rests on the philosophical and Buddhist ideas the text uses, not on any dated record, and the book was completed by Dridhabala centuries later and revised again after him. Where Ayurveda's ideas came from (Vedic ritual healing or ascetic and Buddhist circles) is debated.

people: Agnivesha, legendary author of the original text
Caraka (fl. between c. 100 BCE and 200 CE), editor
Dridhabala (c. 5th century CE), completed the text
Gerrit Jan Meulenbeld, historian whose dating is standard
Kenneth G. Zysk, historian of the ascetic-origins thesis
summary: A book by three authors over several centuries, it set out Ayurveda's theory of three humors, and its origins are still argued over.
body: The oldest surviving complete treatise of classical Indian medicine says plainly that it was written by three people. An early text by Agnivesha was edited by Caraka, and Caraka's work was later completed by Dridhabala. Weighing the philosophical and Buddhist ideas it draws on, the Indologist Jan Meulenbeld concluded that Caraka lived no earlier than about 100 BCE and no later than about 150–200 CE. Dridhabala is placed around the fifth century CE, and Philipp Maas has found manuscript evidence that it may have been revised thoroughly at least once more after him.

Its medicine is practical: diagnosis, diet, drugs and a standard set of five cleansing therapies (emetics, purgatives, two kinds of enema and nasal purging). Behind them stands a theory of three humors, or *doshas*: wind, bile and phlegm. In one chapter a panel of sages argues over whether breath, fire or soma is the cornerstone of health, until the chair, Punarvasu Atreya, rules that it comes down to a balance of the three humors. Caraka even observes that the body's parts cannot be counted, because they are made of atoms too small to perceive.

The text opens with a pedigree: medicine passed from the gods through sages to Agnivesha. Historians read this as the customary frame of a learned Sanskrit treatise, not as a chronicle. Where the ideas really came from is debated. Older accounts traced Ayurveda back to the healing hymns of the Atharvaveda. In 1991 Kenneth Zysk argued that it grew instead among wandering healers and ascetics, Buddhist monks among them, outside Brahmin orthodoxy. Dominik Wujastyk finds that the claimed Vedic parallels break down, judges it almost certain that Ayurveda's foundations were laid in Buddhist and other ascetic communities, and notes that the Buddha is recorded naming wind, bile and phlegm among the causes of disease. The text itself advises a physician who is pressed on the point to say he follows the Atharvaveda, a line Wujastyk reads as diplomacy rather than history.

Its reach was wide. Arabic translations of Indian medical works circulated early, and the physician al-Razi (d. 925) cited Arabic versions of Caraka often. Ayurveda, the tradition it helped found, is backed today by the Indian state with hospitals, colleges and a thriving pharmaceutical industry.

myth.tradition: Ayurveda is a timeless Vedic science, and the Charaka Samhita records knowledge revealed by the gods in remote antiquity.
myth.record: The text took shape between about 100 BCE and 200 CE, was completed around the fifth century and revised later; its divine pedigree is a literary convention, and its debt to Vedic medicine is doubtful.

title: The Sushruta Samhita and Indian surgery

traditional.note: Popular histories and some museum labels still date Sushruta to about 600 BCE, a figure with no support in datable evidence from the text.

confidence.note: The surgical content is plain in the surviving text, but its date is not: the work was composed and revised by several hands, one passage postdates the arrival of Greek astrology in India, and the oldest manuscript is dated 878 CE. Scholars place composition in the early centuries CE, complete by about 500.

people: Sushruta, the authority named in the title, otherwise unknown
Dominik Wujastyk, historian leading the Sushruta Project
summary: Instructions for rebuilding a severed nose with a flap of cheek skin, written in Sanskrit some two thousand years ago, though not as long ago as legend says.
body: Some two thousand years ago, someone writing in Sanskrit set down how to rebuild a severed nose. Cut a leaf to the size of the missing part, slice a matching patch of living flesh from the cheek, scarify it and press it into place, bandage it neatly, and insert two small pipes into the nostrils so the patient can breathe. The passage sits in the Compendium of Sushruta (*Sushruta Samhita*), the fullest account of surgery in early Indian medicine.

The book covers the training of surgeons and the making and care of scalpels, probes and pincers. It describes cutting for bladder stone through the perineum, couching cataracts, reducing dislocations, lancing boils, piercing earlobes, removing foreign bodies, repairing harelip and suturing wounds. Couching meant pushing the clouded lens out of the line of sight with a needle. Done without anesthesia, it left poor vision in an age without spectacles, but that was better than blindness. The learned surgical school did not survive as professional practice, though barber-surgeons kept techniques such as couching alive.

How old is it? Popular accounts, and even some museum labels, say Sushruta wrote around 600 BCE. The text cannot bear such a precise date. Like the other early compendia, it was composed and revised by several hands, and one passage uses the Greek astrological word *hora*, showing that whoever wrote that part knew Hellenistic astrology, which reached India in the second century CE. Current scholarship puts its composition in the early centuries CE, complete by about 500. The oldest surviving copy, a palm-leaf manuscript in Kathmandu announced in 2007, is dated 878 CE and preserves an earlier stage of the text than the printed editions.

Sushruta is often hailed as the father of plastic surgery, and his method is tied directly to the nose repair reported in a London magazine in 1794. The link is looser than it looks. The Sanskrit passage is, in Dominik Wujastyk's words, too "brief and laconic" to follow without a teacher, it uses the cheek rather than the forehead flap of 1794, and the operator then was a man of the brickmaker caste who is unlikely to have had access to Sanskrit manuscripts.

myth.tradition: Sushruta, 'the father of plastic surgery', wrote his Samhita around 600 BCE, and the Indian nose surgeons of 1794 were practicing his method.
myth.record: The text is layered and was probably composed in the early centuries CE; its nose repair uses a cheek flap, not the 1794 forehead flap, and no direct line between the two has been shown.

title: Ashoka's edict on medical care

confidence.note: The edict survives in stone and dates itself to Ashoka's twelfth regnal year; converting that to about 257 BCE depends on the accepted Mauryan chronology. What the words promise is clear; how far the program was carried out is not recorded.

place: Girnar (Gujarat) and other sites across the Mauryan empire
people: Ashoka (d. 232 BCE), Mauryan emperor, styled 'Beloved-of-the-Gods, King Piyadasi'
summary: An emperor carved into rock his promise of medical treatment for people and for animals, with medicinal plants imported where none grew.
body: Around 257 BCE the Mauryan emperor Ashoka had his second Major Rock Edict carved at sites across his empire. In it 'Beloved-of-the-Gods, King Piyadasi' announces two kinds of medical treatment, for humans and for animals, in his realm and among neighbors as far as the lands of the Greek king Antiochos. Where medicinal herbs, roots or fruits were lacking, he had them imported and grown; along roads he had wells dug and trees planted. It is sometimes hailed as founding the first hospitals, but the edict names no buildings at all.

myth.record: Rock Edict II promises medical treatment, medicinal plants, wells and shade trees; it does not mention hospital buildings.

title: The Bower Manuscript

confidence.note: The find and purchase in 1890 are well documented and the manuscript survives. Its date rests only on handwriting: Hoernle first put it in the mid-fifth century and later pushed it earlier, while current estimates span roughly 400 to 600 CE.

people: Lieutenant H. Bower, British officer who bought it
A. F. Rudolf Hoernle, Indologist who deciphered it
summary: Treasure hunters on the Silk Road dug a bundle of birch bark out of a stupa in 1890: some of the oldest Indian medical writing on record.
body: In February 1890 two treasure hunters from Kucha, an oasis on the Silk Road in today's Xinjiang, dug into a ruined stupa and pulled out leaves of birch bark covered in writing. In early March they sold them to Lieutenant H. Bower, a British officer who had come to Kucha hunting a murderer. Deciphered by Rudolf Hoernle, the leaves proved to be Sanskrit, and largely medical: a tract on garlic and a compendium called the *Navanitaka*, copied by a Buddhist. They are practical recipe books, not theory, and they show Indian medicine traveling with Buddhism into Central Asia.

links.note: Classical compendium whose recipes it parallels.

title: Vagbhata's synthesis

confidence.note: Scholars place the Ashtangahridaya shortly after 600 CE on internal and literary evidence rather than a dated record. Its standing as a school text and its wide translation are well attested; details of its author's life, including his religion, are not.

people: Vagbhata (fl. c. 600 CE), physician-author from Sindh
summary: Around 600 CE a physician from Sindh condensed Caraka and Sushruta into the 'Heart of Medicine', the textbook much of Asia would learn from.
body: Shortly after 600 CE a physician from Sindh named Vagbhata composed the *Ashtangahridaya*, the 'Heart of Medicine', which brilliantly condensed the older compendia of Caraka and Sushruta into one work. It was widely adopted as a medical school text, and through many translations and adaptations it became one of the most important medical treatises in Asia. It traveled as Ayurveda did: Tibetan translators from the eighth century onward made Indian medical works part of Tibetan healing. Some historians think Vagbhata may have been a Buddhist.

links.note: Indian medical works shaped Tibetan medicine.
